4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.name: The Italian woman poet and peace activist of Armenian descent Vittoria Aganoor Pompilj (1855–1910), and a signed copy of her poem 'Peace'
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.type: Photograph and autograph collected in a register
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.author: Maria Grazia Bistoni, Costanza Maria Del Giudice
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.archival: AS PG, Società per la pace e l'arbitrato internazionale di Perugia, 10
4be86fc9-7fe9-524a-8ea0-665de458829d.description2: The descendant of an Armenian family that migrated to Venice at the beginning of the 19th century, Vittoria Aganoor Pompilj authored poems that were translated during her life into English, French and Spanish. She corresponded with many international literary figures and was a member of the International Arbitration and Peace League of Perugia (*Società per la pace e l'arbitrato internazionale di Perugia*), founded in 1892. In 1870, the British trade unionist Randal Cremer (Nobel peace laureate in 1907) founded the International Arbitration League, which –among other things – protested British intervention in Egypt and imperialism.

4bf6a5a2-2ef7-5efd-930f-e900942ddaa6.name: *La Péri: thirteen costume sketches*
4bf6a5a2-2ef7-5efd-930f-e900942ddaa6.description2: *La Péri* is a fantastical ballet in two acts with the scenario written by Theophile Gautier and the music by Burgmüller. This ballet, first performed in 1843, brought the audience to a grand Egyptian palace. Théophile Gautier dreamt of visiting Egypt, where his friend Gerard de Nerval had been living and sending him details to help him make the ballet more realistic.

4c7b394a-e1a0-5aff-b896-8caf9feaef32.name: Original sheet music of 'The Portugueza'
4c7b394a-e1a0-5aff-b896-8caf9feaef32.dates: Published in the supplement of the *Ocidente*, n. 405, 21 March 1890
4c7b394a-e1a0-5aff-b896-8caf9feaef32.artist: Henrique Lopes de Mendonça; Alfredo Keil
4c7b394a-e1a0-5aff-b896-8caf9feaef32.description2: Original sheet music of “The Portugueza”, initially a contest song against the British Ultimatum. It became the national anthem after the Republican Revolution.

50134a0e-a943-5f25-a36c-43032ad0dd5e.name: Bob Walter [veiled dancer]
50134a0e-a943-5f25-a36c-43032ad0dd5e.description2: The "serpentine dance", invented by Mary Louise Fuller, was copied by many dancers, and even parodied. Like Fuller, these dancers also used veils and lighting effects, characteristics typical of the Art Nouveau movement.

5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.name: Portrait of Paul Draneht
5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.author: Massimiliano Cremona, Ignazio Galella
5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.second_name: Paul Draneht (1815–1894), the Superintendent of the Cairo Opera who commissioned Aida from Giuseppe Verdi
5213376b-6aff-55de-afcc-32cf7bfb66d1.description2:
Paul Draneht (1815-1894) was born in Nicosia (Cyprus) as Pavlos Pavlidis. He was the child of a Greek Christian Orthodox family who fled Cyprus due to the clashes between Greeks and Turks, and took refuge in Egypt. Muhammad (Mehmet) Ali Pasha (the Khedive of Egypt) sent him to study in France. Trusted by the Khedive (who awarded him the titles of Bey and Pasha), Paul Draneht participated in the negotiations regarding the opening of the Suez Canal.  
He became superintendent of the Egyptian Opera Theatre and commissioned the opera Aida to the Italian composer Giuseppe Verdi. The Aida opened in Cairo on 24 December 1871.

522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.name: Veil
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.author: Huda Kilani
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.keywords: Linen fabric; natural cotton; embroidered patterns
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.materials: Linen, silk; hand weaving, hand embroidered, natural dyes
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.description2: Three natural cotton and linen fabrics sewn and decorated with cross-stitch with embroidered folkloric patterns (known as “cypress trees”, “amulets”, “keys”, “saw” and “Shuayb teeth”). They are mainly in red with some green colour; a small linen fringe dangles from two sides. The veil was an essential piece of women’s dress. Girls started preparing their trousseau (clothes, shawls, and other belongings collected for marriage) at the age of ten. Married women had various embroidered costumes worn for special occasions. As the economy of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th century-early 20th century relied on trades and crafts, new waves of traders and artisans started to arrive and to settle. Thus, traditional costumes reflect a variegated population composition, demographic changes, personal attire and local rites.

5284ca06-d2a1-58f9-b56b-e749fc9d4c22.name: Portrait of Shaykh Ibrahim al-Yaziji
5284ca06-d2a1-58f9-b56b-e749fc9d4c22.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
5284ca06-d2a1-58f9-b56b-e749fc9d4c22.description2: Ibrahim al-Yaziji was born on 2 March 1847 in Beirut. He was educated by his father, Shaykh Nasif, and then in 1872 he became the chief editor of the magazine *al-Najah*. In 1884 he began publishing for *al-Tabib* with Bishara Zalzal and Khalil Sa'adeh. He edited all his father's books, and republished them alongside the *Diwan* of al-Mutanabbi. In 1894 he travelled around Europe, and then settled in Cairo, were he began publishing a new magazine *al-Bayan* and then later *al-Dhiya'*, for eight years. His most famous publication was titled "The Language of Newspapers". He died in Egypt on 28 December 1906.

529b4a95-033c-586c-b6c2-ba606e63c4aa.name: Buzuq
529b4a95-033c-586c-b6c2-ba606e63c4aa.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music
529b4a95-033c-586c-b6c2-ba606e63c4aa.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
529b4a95-033c-586c-b6c2-ba606e63c4aa.keywords: Dabke; Music; Lebanese; Oriental; Hybrid; Sound
529b4a95-033c-586c-b6c2-ba606e63c4aa.description2: The word *buzuq* comes from Turkish. *Bashi-buzuq* for example, literally meaning 'burnt head', was one of the nicknames given to the Ottoman troops. The *buzuq* is of hybrid origin and thus is considered neither a traditional Arabic instrument nor a traditional Turkish instrument. Used for *dabke* music, the instrument was originally associated with the traveller communities in Lebanon. It consists of a long, fretted neck with four sets of double strings, and is played with a plectrum.

52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.name: Amulet
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.type: Cultic Object; ornament; talismanic object; jewellery
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.author: Huda Kilani
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.keywords: Talisman; crescent; tusks; wild boar; heal of Gazalle
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.description2: This object is a piece of horse jewellery, an amulet worn around the horse's neck to ward off misfortune. Horse jewellery was used among Bedouins and villagers communities. This amulet consists of a silver-cased crescent composed of two joined tusks of wild boar. A ¼ Majidi Ottoman gold coin dangles from the crescent with three crescents and stars at the end. The silver chain is called “heal of gazelle”.

5384b8df-a79b-54a7-bdbf-0c4918314519.name: Qanun
5384b8df-a79b-54a7-bdbf-0c4918314519.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music
5384b8df-a79b-54a7-bdbf-0c4918314519.dimensions: H: 4 to 6cm, L: 95 to 100cm, W: 38 to 40cm
5384b8df-a79b-54a7-bdbf-0c4918314519.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
5384b8df-a79b-54a7-bdbf-0c4918314519.description2: The *qanun* is a traditional instrument of the Middle East, whose name in Arabic also means "rule, principle or norm". It has a range of three octaves, and today it is made with nylon or PVC strings are stretched over a single bridge, poised on fish-skins on one end, and attached to tuning pegs on the other. Turkish models have 26 sets of triple strings. It rests on the player's lap and is played by plucking, either with the player's fingernails or with two tortoise-shell plectrums.

541e7afc-c735-5bac-ad3a-928530f9d141.name: Horse adornment used in wedding ceremonies (*Gushnik*)
541e7afc-c735-5bac-ad3a-928530f9d141.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist
541e7afc-c735-5bac-ad3a-928530f9d141.keywords: Horse ornament; monistra; horse jewellery; accessories; marriage; wedding
541e7afc-c735-5bac-ad3a-928530f9d141.description2: A *gushnik* is an article used for the adornment of horses. This item shows the tradition of decorating horses on some festive occasions, particularly on weddings. The decoration consists of a string and numerous ornaments made of *monistra* (tiny beads in varied colours) applied on canvas. The pendants are decorated with varied patterns and have fringes at the bottom.

5426a620-cbfc-5b20-bed9-14fa1801de7d.name: *Medjmouaï teçavir* (Collection de costumes)
5426a620-cbfc-5b20-bed9-14fa1801de7d.keywords: costume; diplomacy; fashion; court life; economy; finance; Ottoman; Tercüman; travel; traveller; Orientalism
5426a620-cbfc-5b20-bed9-14fa1801de7d.description2: Popular postcard from Turkey showing the costume worn by various people, according to occupation, activity, etc. At this time Turkish financial officials worked under European management.

54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.name: Dress
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.author: Huda Kilani
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.materials: Silk, cotton; hand woven Syrian silk fabric (brocade)
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.description2: This dress of al-Druze (Druse) women is made of a long grey with green and silver brocade, pursed narrow sleeves, wide, open square shaped chest, pursed at the middle and wide at the bottom with ruffles and a cotton liner. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation. The traditional Druse and other Jordanian costumes were influenced by the local trade and economic activities: as illustrated in this case, they were often made of silk textiles, produced in Syria and traded to Jordan and Palestine.

54877a94-0bd3-5eff-a7df-cba98f2e5ac9.name: Portrait of 'Abd Allah al-Bustani
54877a94-0bd3-5eff-a7df-cba98f2e5ac9.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
54877a94-0bd3-5eff-a7df-cba98f2e5ac9.description2: 'Abd Allah al-Bustani was born in Debbeye (al-Chouf district) in December 1854, and studied at the National School of Butrus al-Bustani until 1873. He first started teaching in the villages of 'Abeyh and Damur, and then moved to Cyprus, where he published a newspaper. He later returned to Lebanon and taught at the Sagesse College for ten years, and then at the Patriarchal College for 14 years. He wrote many plays, of which only one survives today. His most notable work, however, was the dictionary "al-Bustan". He died in February 1930.

54ee640a-4e1d-59a5-ba23-f9a85bf4e010.name: Gilet
54ee640a-4e1d-59a5-ba23-f9a85bf4e010.holder: Musée Public National des Arts et Traditions Populaires
54ee640a-4e1d-59a5-ba23-f9a85bf4e010.archival: *Algérie, Mémoire de Femmes au Fil des Doigts*, Paris: 2002
54ee640a-4e1d-59a5-ba23-f9a85bf4e010.description2: This velvet bolero, known as a *frimla* has an embroidered front. It was typically worn over a silk shirt. Young Muslim and Jewish girls wore this gilet.

554cc278-49e0-58cd-8147-15ce5f2c7002.name: Lady Layard’s jewellery
554cc278-49e0-58cd-8147-15ce5f2c7002.description2: Layard, excavator of Nineveh and other sites, had this necklace made as a wedding present for his wife. It combines ancient cylinder seals in contemporary gold settings. Said to have been much admired during dinner with Queen Victoria in 1873.

55519584-25f8-5377-bd87-8e67cbc0dc2c.name: Matchlock gun
55519584-25f8-5377-bd87-8e67cbc0dc2c.keywords: Weaponry; weapon; arms; armours; military object; metalwork; dance

557a3c2b-e69e-533d-a2c9-d263db2c8d12.name: Woman's *entari*
557a3c2b-e69e-533d-a2c9-d263db2c8d12.description2: *Entari*s were worn over thin silk shifts and baggy *shalvar* trousers and were held at the waist by a sash or belt. They could be worn open or buttoned above the waist. Several *entari*s, made of different fabrics, usually with contrasting colours, were often layered on top of one another. They were more often than not made of luxurious silk striped or brocaded fabrics and trimmed with fine braid or *oya* needlework.

56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.name: Buckles (*Pafti*)
56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist
56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.keywords: Buckles; live gold-plating; wedding; marriage; accessories; costume
56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.materials: Silver, filigree, granulation. Decoration with semi-precious stones, pearls and live gold plating
56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.description2: Buckles were distinctive articles of adornment used throughout the centuries by Macedonian women. They were the most frequently worn and most exquisite articles of adornment in Macedonian women’s folk attire. Buckles used to be adorned with stylized geometric and floral patterns, the artistic effect having been emphasized by the application of decorative stones, filigree ornaments, gold-plating, pearls, mother-of-pearl, corals, chains and other embellishments. This outstanding set of buckles in leaf shapes is decorated with pearls and semi-precious stones, by application of the technique of "live" gold-plating.

5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.name: Wedding dress
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.author: Huda Kilani
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.materials: Linen and silk; hand woven and hand embroidered
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.description2: Long black dress, wide at the bottom with narrow sleeves, rounded neck and open chest. Silk linen appliqué, hand embroidery with cross-stitch on the sides, back panel, chest, and sleeves with embroidered folkloric patterns. On the chest: necklace, cypress tree. Side: ivy, amulets, “feathers”. Front: small cypress tree on silk. Back: ivy, cypress tree, pillows, pasha tents. Sleeve: ivy, feather, triangle (amulets). Palestinian women's costumes varied according to each Palestinian city and geographical area. Costumes in the mountain regions were different from those of coastal and desert areas, and had a distinguished embroidery. This costume represents village style. Girls started preparing their trousseau (clothes, shawls and other belongings they collected for their marriage) at the age of ten. Married women's costumes were heavily embroidered. Palestinian weavers used traditional spinning processes using manual spindles to prepare the cotton and linen threads imported from Egypt. Ashkelon city weavers used light vertical hand looms (*Majdalawi* looms) to produce linen fabrics, while silk fabrics were spindled and woven in Syria.

593969dc-7368-5182-961d-c81a464474fc.name: Bridal headdress (*Kiska*)
593969dc-7368-5182-961d-c81a464474fc.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist
593969dc-7368-5182-961d-c81a464474fc.keywords: Decorative pin; kiska; apotropaic intention; amulet; talisman; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; wedding; marriage
593969dc-7368-5182-961d-c81a464474fc.description2: Hairpins and other articles of adornment worn on the head were inevitable elements of Macedonian women's attire in the 19th century and at the beginning of the 20th century. This distinctive decorative pin – *kiska* – was used for supporting the hat or scarf. This type of jewellery also conveyed a symbolic meaning and served an apotropaic purpose in addition to its decorative function. The pear-shaped ornament was made by application of filigree and granulation techniques. It is adorned with pellets and decorative stones in varied colours. Tiny coins are suspended on chains at the bottom of the ornament.

5984df39-df0b-5179-8186-0d620e962e8c.name: Portrait of Butrus al-Bustani
5984df39-df0b-5179-8186-0d620e962e8c.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
5984df39-df0b-5179-8186-0d620e962e8c.description2: Butrus al-Bustani was born in Debbeye, and studied at Ayn Warka School for ten years. He was appointed professor at this school at the age of 20, before moving to teach in the American College of 'Abeyh. He then moved to Beirut, where he became an interpreter at the US consulate, working with American missionaries and their printing press. He published numerous important books, including his famous Encyclopedia, and founded the National School of Beirut. He died in May 1883.

59da1fe4-84c5-5f28-93ff-51acc78bc1c4.name: *Young Algerian man*
59da1fe4-84c5-5f28-93ff-51acc78bc1c4.description2: Much of what was written about life in Algiers during the 18th and 19th centuries focussed on the elegance of male dress. This lithographic illustrated page is taken from a collection entitled *Costumes Nationaux* which was published simultaneously in both London and Paris. It shows a young Algerian man, wearing a red *chechia* with a blue tassel, a large *sarouel* tied at the waist by a long cotton belt, and a long-sleeved embroidered *ghlila*. He is leaning on a *skemla* with a nargile pipe on top. However, even in this image the model does not have a very Algerian appearance. This was a common occurrence, as European artists would complete their works in their studios after having returned from their travels.

59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.name: Belt
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.author: Huda Kilani
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.keywords: Leather; belt; embellished; niello; rosette buckles; silver
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.description2: Leather belt embellished with silver pieces decorated in niello with patterns and symbols at the end. Two silver rosette buckles at the end form a locking mechanism. This is an object produced by Circassian craftsmen. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries, with which they had spiritual and religious links. They brought with them their traditional activities, crafts and decorative patterns. All these elements soon mingled with the local Arab society and became part of the social and economic landscape of the Arab countries.

59e91077-81f0-5cb2-9fc1-2e7eb98c95ab.name: Turkish woman
59e91077-81f0-5cb2-9fc1-2e7eb98c95ab.description2: The Zangaki brothers were a pair of photographers working in Egypt who sold "Orientalist" photos to Western tourists. This photograph for example, responds to Western stereotypes by depicting a Turkish woman lying nonchalantly by shisha pipe.

5c6bfb8e-5045-5559-8078-f4e37350944b.name: Pillowcase
5c6bfb8e-5045-5559-8078-f4e37350944b.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
5c6bfb8e-5045-5559-8078-f4e37350944b.description2: Textiles and embroidery found a wide array of uses which reflect the imaginations of Turkish women. In these textiles, silk, golden and silver threads were used for embroidery. From the 18th and 19th century on – when Western influence started – almost every colour found use and by using different tones of the same colour, the illusion of light and depth was created. Instead of human and animal figures, floral design, fruits, or calligraphy, ship and architectural patterns became more popular. This piece was made in the Hereke Plant, founded in 1843. There is one big star and crescent in the middle while there are four smaller ones in the corners. The base is covered with plenty of stars and dots.

5cada7e5-c863-5bd3-ae0b-41ec4765404d.name: *Grand Vizier*
5cada7e5-c863-5bd3-ae0b-41ec4765404d.keywords: costume; Orientalism; drawing; travel; traveller; fashion; court life
5cada7e5-c863-5bd3-ae0b-41ec4765404d.description2: Sheet from *Costumes Turcs*, a lavish set of volumes produced in Turkey for a European audience. They present the appearance of people from different areas, with different jobs etc.

5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.name: Brass head of flagpole
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.author: Huda Kilani
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.keywords: crescent shape; casted brass; wooden staff
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.description2: A crescent shape made of casted brass fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

5f40f57f-eab0-5e59-ab8b-a946c85ff75c.name: Woman in traditional dress, Jardin d'Essai

5f944369-bc84-59f2-a3a6-21c5dda0f6fe.name: Wooden clogs
5f944369-bc84-59f2-a3a6-21c5dda0f6fe.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
5f944369-bc84-59f2-a3a6-21c5dda0f6fe.description2: Wooden clogs such as these have a long history in the Middle East, emerging before the Middle Ages and remaining popular for centuries to come. They were made of a variety of woods, including walnut, apricot, willow, poplar, or beech. The wood was cut into wedge shapes then moulded around the foot of the wearer. Excess wood was then shaved off, the heel attached, and the wood painted and polished. Leather girdles in a variety of colours were fixed to the heel with special nails and the wood would often be decorated with mosaics of bone or seashells organised in geometric or floral patterns. Clogs were designed to be comfortable and resistant to water, and thus were usually worn at home, particularly by women. These shoes have a higher heel than usual and would be worn by brides so that they would appear taller than the other girls in the *hammam* (Turkish baths).

5f958fd8-3a2a-50d4-a26a-9ea8b55e677e.name: Gilet
5f958fd8-3a2a-50d4-a26a-9ea8b55e677e.author: Houria Cherid
5f958fd8-3a2a-50d4-a26a-9ea8b55e677e.archival: "D'Ikossim à el-Djazayir", in *Catalogue d'Exposition du Musée Public National des Antiquités, 2007*
5f958fd8-3a2a-50d4-a26a-9ea8b55e677e.description2: Men's sleeveless gilet, embroidered with gold thread.

602e2e1a-614b-533b-b171-c2a7bb60bc72.name: Bridal apron
602e2e1a-614b-533b-b171-c2a7bb60bc72.dates: End of the19th – beginning of the 20th century
602e2e1a-614b-533b-b171-c2a7bb60bc72.author: Gordanche Vidinic, ethnologist
602e2e1a-614b-533b-b171-c2a7bb60bc72.keywords: Plain weave; warp; weft; sequins; sash; costume; accessories; textile; shell; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; wedding; marriage
602e2e1a-614b-533b-b171-c2a7bb60bc72.materials: Plain weave of cotton warp and weft consisting of wool and silver and gold wrapped thread. Decoration with sequins – *svetlinke*, *puloi*, and beads
602e2e1a-614b-533b-b171-c2a7bb60bc72.second_name: Apron with sash and bead chain
602e2e1a-614b-533b-b171-c2a7bb60bc72.description2: Belts, sashes and aprons were unavoidable accessories of folk costumes in all areas of Macedonia. This sash was made of white hand-woven cotton cloth, which was decorated at the front with embroidery of pink wool, silver-wrapped thread, silver string, sequins and multi-coloured beads. It has a hook and a loop on the ends for fastening. The apron was made in the technique of plain-weave. The warp of cotton and the weft of red wool and silver and gold-wrapped threads was embellished with sequins – *svetlinke* – and beads. The apron has two strips on the left and right sides woven and decorated in the same manner with shells and coins suspended at the bottom.

60c41d82-4ce0-5ec0-9037-67792716aba8.name: Tunic (*'aba'a*)
60c41d82-4ce0-5ec0-9037-67792716aba8.description: Aba or man’s robe is inspired in the North African ones. It is made in cream velvet with a stencilled decoration related with Safavid motifs. This kind of garment that Fortuny discovered in his travels for North Africa is related to Spanish Muslim “aljubas” of the Medieval Spain.
60c41d82-4ce0-5ec0-9037-67792716aba8.holder: Museum of Costume, Ethnographical Heritage Research Centre
60c41d82-4ce0-5ec0-9037-67792716aba8.author: Elvira González
60c41d82-4ce0-5ec0-9037-67792716aba8.keywords: Costumes; Design; North African influence; Spanish Muslim influence

61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.name: Traditional peasant attire
61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.materials: The costumes were made of cotton and silk
61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.second_name: Villager from the Beqaa Valley in traditional dress
61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.description2: Peasants and ordinary people's clothes did not change much over the centuries. It generally consisted of a shorter, narrower and darker coloured pair of baggy *shirwal* trousers for winter, and another pair in a lighter beige or khaki colour for the summer. This was paired with a cotton shirt or vest, called a *sudriye*, and a short embroidered *abaya*. A *keffiye*, a large scarf made of white cotton, was worn on the head with a *lebbede* or *'agal* on top.

6204d094-907f-5ef3-b378-936a43e07247.name: An Entertainment Scene (The third day of entertainment) from *Surname-i Vehbi*
6204d094-907f-5ef3-b378-936a43e07247.archival: The Library of Sultan Ahmed III
6204d094-907f-5ef3-b378-936a43e07247.description2: These images show events that took place on the Golden Horn on the evening of the third day. In them, we see the sultan seated in a tent on the Arsenal Palace quay surrounded by attendants. Two rafts are floating by. The one at the right, of which we can only see a part but appears to be a platform mounted on a pair of caiques, was donated by Yeğen Mehmed Pasha, Superintendent of the Customs Office. The figures of two rams suspended on gears and pulleys from the roof butt one another. This is following a real raft on which are set two gigantic dummies that face backwards and are dressed in Persian garb. At the front of the raft is a huge wheel of fireworks that one of the pyrotechnicists is causing to revolve. Its supporting frame is surmounted by a fire-spewing bird and rockets hurtle this way and that.

6361ef20-5b25-59b2-bd56-7f7ed9244291.name: Reed pipe
6361ef20-5b25-59b2-bd56-7f7ed9244291.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
6361ef20-5b25-59b2-bd56-7f7ed9244291.author: Huda Kilani
6361ef20-5b25-59b2-bd56-7f7ed9244291.description2: A pair of blank reeds opened from both sides, of moderate thickness. Each has six holes on the surface attached together with a type of gum. Playing the *mijwiz* requires some ability because it is played by blowing into both reeds at the same time and pushing the air strongly with the cheeks. Shepherds used to play it while taking their flocks of sheep and goats to graze. It is a popular traditional musical instrument in the Middle East.

640cbdc1-fd31-5fad-89d3-4deff3b9943f.name: Municipal theatre
640cbdc1-fd31-5fad-89d3-4deff3b9943f.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
640cbdc1-fd31-5fad-89d3-4deff3b9943f.history: This building, which was once the Municipal Casino and often affectionately known as the "bonbonnière Resplandy", was built in the early 20th century in the Art Nouveau style by the French Architect Jean-Émile Resplandy and located on Avenue Jules-Ferry (now Avenue Habib-Bourguiba) in the heart of the European quarter. It has been constantly active since its birth, clearing the way for new artistic talent. The biggest names in Tunisian and Arab performing arts stood on its stage, performing ballet, opera, dramatic performances, classical concerts and more. In 2011 it became an important symbol of the Tunisian revolution; protestors, martyrs and rebels from all sides stood on its steps at some point.
640cbdc1-fd31-5fad-89d3-4deff3b9943f.keywords: Art Nouveau; theatre; stucco; bas reliefs; Apollo
640cbdc1-fd31-5fad-89d3-4deff3b9943f.description2: This theatre, the last remnant of a municipal artistic complex, can hold up to 1,350 seats. An immense white building, it reflects the style of Art Nouveau with evidence for some baroque influences. The bas-relief decorations, showing a scene with Apollo and the two muses, dominate the façade. The interior, from the vestibule to foyer, is notable for its modern structure and the richness of the carved stucco decorations. The bas-reliefs, moulds, cornices and balconies were all made by famous French and Italian artists.

647bb6c0-14ae-506b-85c5-060226c34178.name: Poet Nigar Hanım
647bb6c0-14ae-506b-85c5-060226c34178.description2: Nigar Hanım, who was born in Istanbul in 1856, studied in a French school. She also took private Turkish, Arabic and Persian classes. She started to write poems when she was a child. She had a very good command of the French language and French literature. Every Tuesday, she gathered reputable personalities at her place, where they discussed art and literature, listened to music and read poems. She collected her poems in *Efsûs I* (1877), *Efsûs II* (1891), *Nîram* (1896), *Aks-i Seda* (1900) and *Elhan-i Vatan* (1916). She also wrote a work of prose in 1901 entitled *Safahat-i Kalb*. A fine lyricism that expresses her unhappiness in her private life can be observed in her work. Among the Turkish poets, she was the most productive, writing very original pieces in the second half of the 19th century.

65d5d950-d069-5d9e-989f-ca9b3eb57b29.name: *Harem*
65d5d950-d069-5d9e-989f-ca9b3eb57b29.description2: Pascal Sébah (1823–1886) was a French photographer working in the Ottoman Empire. This photo of a harem is interesting insofar as it  differs from the mainstream representations of harems in the Western imagination, which were influenced by the painter Gérôme. Indeed, many local customs - both real and imagined - captured the interest of European artists, and their Orientalist art then fuelled both the Western fascination with and revulsion towards the East.

665fead3-3926-5df0-ac85-fe2c13fabcb2.name: *Bisht muqassab*
665fead3-3926-5df0-ac85-fe2c13fabcb2.description2: A clothing article, made out of cotton, worn during weddings.

680c8cb0-7e03-52b8-988d-a7e74dbb89fa.name: *L'Égyptienne*, military operetta in three acts and 11 scenes.
680c8cb0-7e03-52b8-988d-a7e74dbb89fa.description2: Egypt became the subject of choice across the theatrical arts as a symptom of "Egyptomania", a phenomenon which spanned the length of the 19th century. This military operetta, written by de Chivot, Nuitter and Beaumont (with music by Charles Lecocq) is set in Egypt during the arrival of the Napoleonic troops.

68850fe9-86ff-5692-8ae9-7d758c18ca87.name: *Letta Asım Baloya Giderken* (*Letta Asım was about to go to a ball*)
68850fe9-86ff-5692-8ae9-7d758c18ca87.holder: Mimar Sinan Fine Arts Unıversity Painting and Sculpture Museum
68850fe9-86ff-5692-8ae9-7d758c18ca87.keywords: Women; women painters; Turkish women painters; Ottoman women painters; women condition; social change; dance; opera; theatre; ballet
68850fe9-86ff-5692-8ae9-7d758c18ca87.description2: As a result of modernization efforts and the increase in relations with the West in the 19th century, there were significant changes in Ottoman social life. Instead of the traditional 18th-century entertainment which consisted of miniatures, in Tanzimat Period of the 19th century, theatre, opera, musical performances and ballrooms became popular in Istanbul. In public places, western-style dance and musical instruments began to be seen.

696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.name: Pin, plaque
696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.author: Huda Kilani
696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.description2: A gold pin with three gold ¼ rashadi Ottoman coins welded together; at the end of two chains hang ¼ gold rashadi coins (Sultan Rashadi, 1909), each with a heart shape dangling from it. Ottoman coins were used as decorative objects for jewellery. Gold jewellery was usually bought only by the rich, while most people used silver jewellery. Pieces of gold or silver jewellery were given by the groom to the bride as a dowry, thus the choice of a piece of jewellery indicated the financial status of the groom.

699fbe74-5142-545f-991c-73824a07527f.name: Author Tevfik Fikret and his book of poetry *Rübab-ı Şikeste*
699fbe74-5142-545f-991c-73824a07527f.description2: Tevfik Fikret, who published his first book of poetry *Rubab-ı Şikeste* (broken instrument), dealt with love, piety, nature and a worldview that was self-enclosed to the environment. His poems influenced other Turkish poets and he is considered a pioneer of contemporary Turkish poetry. His work also has some seeds of the social opposition of the future.

69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.name: Marius Scalesi
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.holder: Institut Culturel Italien (Italian Emabassy in Tunisia)
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.keywords: Marius Scalesi; literature in French; poetry; migration
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.description2: Pictured here is Marius (Mario) Scalesi, a young poet of Italian origin, born on 6 February 1892 in Tunis to an Italian father and a Maltese mother. He suffered from tuberculosis from birth, and became paralysed following a fall down the stairs in his home in La Goulette, the so-called "Little Sicily" of Tunis. Forced to abandon his studies in order to make a living, he completed his education independently. His articles of literary criticism and poems were published in the journal *La Tunisie Illustrée*. His collection of poems, *Les Poèmes d'un Maudit* sheds light on the hardships of his life. He died in 1922 in an asylum in Palermo. A fascinating figure due to his triple cultural identity - Italian, French and Tunisian - he is considered one of the pioneers of North African poetry in French.

6c5fc9c1-bb88-513e-a896-4dd682e2510a.name: Pera Palace Hotel
6c5fc9c1-bb88-513e-a896-4dd682e2510a.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
6c5fc9c1-bb88-513e-a896-4dd682e2510a.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; Ancient Istanbul; hotel; travelling
6c5fc9c1-bb88-513e-a896-4dd682e2510a.description2: Pera Palace Hotel was built in 1892 for the purpose of hosting the passengers of the Orient Express and was named after its location. Alexander Vallaury, a French-Turkish architect living in the city designed the hotel in a blend of neo-classical, art nouveau and oriental styles. The hotel was the first building in Turkey to be powered by electricity other than the Ottoman Palaces. It was also the only address in the city to provide hot running water for its guests and was home to the first electric elevator in Istanbul.

6d50fc9a-40d7-5903-b14d-ddd9bf5e5e84.name: Jacket
6d50fc9a-40d7-5903-b14d-ddd9bf5e5e84.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
6d50fc9a-40d7-5903-b14d-ddd9bf5e5e84.description2: Yusuf Bey Karam's military uniform. It is made of red velvet and embroidered with a yellow gilded thread.

6e335928-9fa2-5b6f-93cb-9088b371f464.name: *Zabun*
6e335928-9fa2-5b6f-93cb-9088b371f464.description2: The *zabun* is similar to a European coat and the Turkish *qaftan* (a European inspired coat). It is speculated that it first arrived in the eastern part of Saudi Arabia through the Hajj, at the time of the Turkish empire, and later became popular in Qatar and Bahrayn. The *zabun* is made out of fine Indian Kashmiri brown wool with intricate embroidery. Decoration: made of light brown wool embroidered with *boteh* design, motif across the coat – paisley, Islamic decorative arts. Imitated because the shape is Kashmiri, shaped like cashew nut, pronounced ‘Gazorah.’ Colours are red, yellow, and edges are lined with metal silk thread – round neck opening. Narrow Nehru collar, or Chinese collar is known in Qatar. Buttons are handmade metal balls down the front. It is worn with the *thawb ishlahat*.

6f83b69e-bc0a-5955-8a8f-46818fc39f26.name: *Chechia maker*
6f83b69e-bc0a-5955-8a8f-46818fc39f26.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
6f83b69e-bc0a-5955-8a8f-46818fc39f26.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
6f83b69e-bc0a-5955-8a8f-46818fc39f26.archival: Tunis au XIXe Siècle: Aquarelles et Textes de Charles Lallemand, Apollonia, 2001.
6f83b69e-bc0a-5955-8a8f-46818fc39f26.description2: This copy of a beautiful watercolour from Charles Lallemand's book *Tunis et ses Environs* shows a Tunisian artisan making a chechia. Before the competition of European industry arose in the 19th century, Tunisian artisans had been the main suppliers of the Middle East.

6f8705b6-8b55-55ab-a02e-52dedab4e4de.name: Long-sleeve women's coat (*Mintan*)
6f8705b6-8b55-55ab-a02e-52dedab4e4de.author: Nada Andonovska
6f8705b6-8b55-55ab-a02e-52dedab4e4de.keywords: Mintan; srma; silk; silver; costume; Yörük community; nomads; Turkish; marriage; wedding
6f8705b6-8b55-55ab-a02e-52dedab4e4de.materials: Decoration with braids and cords of gold wrapped thread
6f8705b6-8b55-55ab-a02e-52dedab4e4de.description2: The enclave of the Turkish Yoruk community in Macedonia living in the mountain villages of Dojran – Valandovo and Radovish – and the Shtip region is a genuine treasure of tangible and intangible heritage that adds to the diversity of traditional culture in Macedonia. This bridal attire preserves some of the traditions in clothing and embellishment of Yoruk women in Macedonia in the 19th century and the early 20th century. A *mintan* is a short upper garment worn over the tunic. This piece is made of red silk. It is decorated with braids and cords of *srma* – gold-wrapped thread applied on the hems and over the front.

6fa4350a-7cda-52e2-97c1-1c3d881b5df8.name: A reproduction of the painting *A Cafe in Istanbul*

6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.name: Organ Made in Tunis by the Italian Firm Cesare Trionfo and Exhibited in Milan
6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.author: Giulia Barrera
6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 197.
6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.third_name: *Organo costruito a Tunisi dalla Ditta Cesare Trionfo ed esposto a Milano*
6faa2e57-f95c-52d9-a61f-402154b53322.description2:
Cesare Trionfo was a child when he migrated with his family to Tunisia from Livorno in 1855. He became a trader, and in 1886 he started trading musical instruments. In Tunis, he later also started a shop that made musical instruments such as this organ. Trionfo promoted the construction of the theatre Politeama Roissini, which he co-owned.  
This organ was exhibited in Milan for the 1906 international exhibition. The organ is a traditional Italian musical instrument. This one has decorative elements taken from Arab architecture.

701d0273-bf02-5200-8f32-6dab9287106b.name: Bridal apron jewellery (*Mangura*)
701d0273-bf02-5200-8f32-6dab9287106b.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist
701d0273-bf02-5200-8f32-6dab9287106b.keywords: Mangura; filigree; perforation; silver; costume; accessories; wedding; marriage
701d0273-bf02-5200-8f32-6dab9287106b.materials: Silver, silver alloy, tiny beads, hammering, casting, filigree, perforation
701d0273-bf02-5200-8f32-6dab9287106b.description2: The influences of Eastern art in Macedonia were largely expressed in the jewellery of the 19th century through the so-called Levantine Baroque style. This piece preserves evidence of the exceptional diversity of the jewellery. Worn on the apron, it also shows that articles of adornment used to be applied on many different items of clothing. A *mangura* consists of a string of tiny beads adorned with ornaments. The larger central pendant has been made in the filigree technique and embellished with decorative stones. It is flanked by minor ornaments decorated by perforation.

70d8300c-308e-5b69-9c40-e4c3750f6ab8.name: Photograph of a musician holding a violin and bow
70d8300c-308e-5b69-9c40-e4c3750f6ab8.description: A photograph of a musician in Morocco, he wears local dress and is holding a violin and bow.
70d8300c-308e-5b69-9c40-e4c3750f6ab8.keywords: Moroccan music; Arab music; musical instrument; violin; ensemble; traditional ensemble; concert; entertainment; traditional music; European musical instruments

7145d9d7-3f20-55d9-a385-486cd31761ab.name: Women's pants (*Don*)
7145d9d7-3f20-55d9-a385-486cd31761ab.author: Nada Andonovska
7145d9d7-3f20-55d9-a385-486cd31761ab.keywords: costume; embroidery; geometric patterns; geometric motifs; Yörük community; nomads; Turkish; marriage; wedding
7145d9d7-3f20-55d9-a385-486cd31761ab.materials: White canvas decorated with embroidery og varied wool, as well as silver and gold wrapped thread
7145d9d7-3f20-55d9-a385-486cd31761ab.description2: The enclave of the Turkish Yoruk community in Macedonia living in the mountain villages of Dojran – Valandovo and Radovish – and the Shtip region is a genuine treasure of tangible and intangible heritage that adds to the diversity of traditional culture in Macedonia. In general terms, the traditional outfit of Yoruk women in Macedonia is distinguished with exceptional colouring and application of varied elements in all articles of clothing. This bridal attire preserves some of the traditions in clothing and embellishment of Yoruk women in Macedonia in the 19th century and the early 20th century. This piece of trousers shows decoration of embroidery with geometric patterns applied on the lower front part of the trousers.

714736c9-97a7-5e87-b9d2-fc5d38aed09f.name: Thirty belts
714736c9-97a7-5e87-b9d2-fc5d38aed09f.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
714736c9-97a7-5e87-b9d2-fc5d38aed09f.description2: Belts like these were traditionally given to a bride by her parents, and were worn for the marriage ceremony. The belts are made of silver, and each one is carved with its tribe's traditional design. The bride would wear the belt of her own tribe during the ceremony as a sign of belonging. These belts date to the 19th century.

71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.name: Daff
71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music
71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
71d1bb15-43f9-5e5d-8a1d-7e157badf90e.description2: The *daff*, also known as the *rikk*, is a popular instrument similar to a tambourine. It is made of a round wooden frame, covered on one side with goat or fish skin. Pairs of metal discs are set into the frame to produce a jingling sound when the instrument is struck. It is used to set the rhythm in many traditional Arabic songs, particularly during purely instrumental performances.

73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.name: Headdress
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.author: Huda Kilani
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.keywords: silver; prominent dome; disk; al- Druz women
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.description2: A silver circular disk with filigree work and prominent dome above; chains dangling with triple petal and filigree work at the end; placed on the top of a high hat worn by al-Druze (Druse) women. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and the demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

7474b893-ab5b-5cb0-8dbf-1f03e7b4dcb1.name: Egyptianising pendant
7474b893-ab5b-5cb0-8dbf-1f03e7b4dcb1.description2: The pendant's rich design illustrates the influence of Egyptian motifs on Victorian jewellery. This piece was based on one made for the British Princess Alexandra.

7482dc94-0a66-563c-a048-83788106efb4.name: Portrait of Shaykh Yusuf al-Asir
7482dc94-0a66-563c-a048-83788106efb4.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
7482dc94-0a66-563c-a048-83788106efb4.description2: Shaykh Yusuf al-Asir was born in Saida in 1815. He studied first in Damascus then in Cairo for seven years, and excelled at Arabic language, *hadith* studies, poetry, and logic. After his studies he returned to Lebanon, going first to Saida then to Tripoli, where he stayed for 3 years. He became the Mufti of 'Akkar, and then served as the general prosecutor of Mount Lebanon for seven years. He then moved to Istanbul, where he became a professor at the Teachers College. Upon his return to Beirut he began teaching at the National College, Sagesse College, and the American School. He also published many literary and religious works in his lifetime, and edited a number of newspapers such as *Lisan al-Hal* and *Thamarat al-Funun*. He died on 28 November 1889.

75891604-fdb8-540e-af25-a6509a9103f7.name: *Cairo: houses and gardens in the French quarter.* Flaubert in the foreground.
75891604-fdb8-540e-af25-a6509a9103f7.description2: The writer Gustave Flaubert lived in Egypt for three years from 1849 to 1851 with his friend Maxime Du Camp. He saw and experienced many new things during this time, travelling to Egypt, Beirut, Jerusalem and Damascus. Although Gustave Flaubert did not like being photographed, Maxime du Camp was able to take this snap of him in Cairo.

75e14725-44b8-5dc0-b587-1eba09b78832.name: Yıldız Palace Theatre
75e14725-44b8-5dc0-b587-1eba09b78832.notice: This is an unedited Database entry and may contain errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are working to raise the funds required to complete the editing; should you wish to contribute please visit our [Support page](https://www.museumwnf.org/atrium_support.php).
75e14725-44b8-5dc0-b587-1eba09b78832.history:
Yildiz Palace, which is the last architectural example of Turkish Ottoman palace, is located on the Yildiz hill in the district of Besiktas. Sultan Ahmed I was the first to build a pavilion, over this land registered at the time to the Private treasury of the Ottoman Sultan as a hunting place sultans beginning during the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566).  
The main construction in the palace started in the period of Sultan Abdulhamid II (1876-1909) and it was called Saray-i Humayun (Central palace). During this period the palace comprised of buildings for private use of the sultan as well as buildings, allocated for the officials, repair shops and carpentry like repairing shop, carpenter’s shop and the buildings of culture and art such as theatre, museum and library. The Palace begun to serve as a museum under the name of Directorate of the Museum of Yildiz Palace since 1993.
75e14725-44b8-5dc0-b587-1eba09b78832.description2: This is the only palace theatre that can be seen today. It was built by the Sultan Abdulhamid II for the visit of German Imperial Kaiser Wilhem II, together with the Shale Kiosk in 1899. Three walls of the theatre hall, of a small rectangular plan, are surrounded by the boxes carried by columns. The box that faced the stage belonged to the sultan. The walls were decorated with hand-drawn and the ceiling was endowed with gold star patterns on the blue ground. Oil paintings are hung around the stage. In addition to performer groups consisting of Italian and Turkish artists, foreign theatre groups visiting Istanbul and some local artists were also occasionally allowed to the palace. Among them, there were French artists, Sarah Bernhardt and Coquelain Cadet and Russian singer Feodor Chaliapin, local artists Gullu Agop Efendi and Nashit Efendi. In the theatre the operas such as Barber of Sevil, Norma, Rigoletto, Traviata, Carmen and Aida were put on stage. The original wardrobes representing the period of use are exhibited in a section of the theatre.

77fc77a2-454c-58fa-aa16-959029610bb1.name: Women's tunic (*Gomlek*)
77fc77a2-454c-58fa-aa16-959029610bb1.author: Nada Andonovska
77fc77a2-454c-58fa-aa16-959029610bb1.keywords: Yörük community; nomads; Turkish; tunic; costume; embroidery; wedding; marriage
77fc77a2-454c-58fa-aa16-959029610bb1.materials: White canvas decorated with embroidery og varied wool, as well as silver and gold wrapped thread
77fc77a2-454c-58fa-aa16-959029610bb1.description2: The enclave of the Turkish Yoruk community in Macedonia living in the mountain villages of Dojran – Valandovo and Radovish – and the Shtip region is a genuine treasure of tangible and intangible heritage that adds to the diversity of traditional culture in Macedonia. In general terms, the traditional outfit of Yoruk women in Macedonia is distinguished with exceptional colouring and application of varied elements in all articles of clothing. This bridal attire preserves some of the traditions in clothing and embellishment of Yoruk women in Macedonia in the 19th century and the early 20th century. The tunic is made of white canvas and modestly decorated by embroidery of two short vertical strips above the lower hem.

7821de49-1833-5656-935a-de7859fecc1b.name: Jacket
7821de49-1833-5656-935a-de7859fecc1b.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
7821de49-1833-5656-935a-de7859fecc1b.description2: Yusuf Bey Karam's jacket, probably worn during the winter months. It is made of dark blue wool, with floral patterns embroidered in black thread and bordered by a black ribbon. The lining is made of a mustard-coloured fabric.

78ffdbad-67b9-5e33-ad6b-19aeeee48f10.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music

78ffdbad-67b9-5e33-ad6b-19aeeee48f10.description2: Mitri al-Murr was a famous musician, well known throughout the Arab world. He was a renowned pianist and wrote a number of musical poems that are still known today.

79fded3c-fc12-5fa3-bff4-6820a231b3e4.name: Marriage shawl
79fded3c-fc12-5fa3-bff4-6820a231b3e4.holder: Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires
79fded3c-fc12-5fa3-bff4-6820a231b3e4.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
79fded3c-fc12-5fa3-bff4-6820a231b3e4.description2: This loose marriage shawl is decorated with various symbols of fertility. Two large rectangles of red wool are sewn together, and their joining seam is ornately decorated with gold embroidery. The decorations are spread out across the whole cloth, forming a strip of finely woven motifs in the centre, which is surrounded by various traditional figures and patterns. The human figures are characteristic of the (often enigmatic) decorative arts of the towns of El Jem and Ouerdanine, and feature here in addition to the more common motifs such as the fish, the hand, disks, circles, diamonds, crescents, the dove and the camel.

7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.name: Record of the marriage between the Egyptian governmental official Paul Draneht Bey, aged 55, and the Italian Adele Casati, aged 19, celebrated in Oggebbio (Italy) in 1873
7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.author: Massimiliano Cremona, Ignazio Galella
7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.archival: AS VB, Comune di Oggebbio, Registro Atti di Matrimonio, vol. 523/24, firme degli sposi
7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.description2: Apparently, Adelaide Casati and her sister Margarita attended the premiere of the Aida in Cairo (24 December 1871). Their father, Filippo, was participating in the performance as a cello player. In Cairo, the two Casati sisters met their future husbands, respectively, Paul Draneht, and the Greek banker, Joannis Sinadino (who acted as witness in the marriage between Paul Draneht and Adelaide Casati). Both men moved to live in Oggebbio, Italy, when Paul Draneht bought a villa there.

7bd75a35-d206-5701-b425-b077957ef154.name: Émile Zola. *J'accuse!* … 11-13 January 1898
7bd75a35-d206-5701-b425-b077957ef154.description2: In 1894, the French army officer Alfred Dreyfus was accused of espionage, found guilty, fired and deported. His family, who were fighting to have him pardoned, won over the famous naturalist writer, Émile Zola. In just a few days, Zola wrote an indictment ("J'accuse"), addressed to the President of the French Republic, which was published in *l'Aurore*.

7c628f29-8443-5e2e-8926-884729f02df3.name: Legged violin
7c628f29-8443-5e2e-8926-884729f02df3.description2: The Violin was not a popular instrument in 16th century except among patrons of taverns. In the early 19th century, musicians used both types of violin – the legged violin and the sine or "chest" violin – but the sine violin disappeared afterwards. The legged violin has a cylindrical body with a relatively long handle. The cut body is made of coconut shell and covered with leather.

7f865df5-a1bf-51f2-943d-4a9bec647c8f.name: Dress
7f865df5-a1bf-51f2-943d-4a9bec647c8f.holder: Musée Public National des Arts et Traditions Populaires
7f865df5-a1bf-51f2-943d-4a9bec647c8f.description2: This long dress or *djebba* is made of brocade and has a breast plate on the front. The low-cut sleeves are bordered by a golden ribbon. Jewish women from Constantine wore this long dress, whereas Muslim women wore a slightly shorter one. Although the decoration of the Constantine dress is completely different today, the shape and cut has not changed.

823a405a-b8cf-5eeb-af76-1bb8e28081d7.name: First issue of *Al-Ahram*
823a405a-b8cf-5eeb-af76-1bb8e28081d7.notice: This is an unedited Database entry and may contain errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are doing our best to complete the editing asap. 823a405a-b8cf-5eeb-af76-1bb8e28081d7.description2:
*Al-Ahram* was founded in Alexandria in 1875 by two Lebanese brothers, Bishara Takla and Salim Takla. It began as a weekly newspaper published every Saturday. Its first issue appeared on 5 August 1876. The paper was relaunched as a daily newspaper in January 1881.  
Its headquarters was in Alexandria until November 1899 when it was moved to Cairo. The newspaper was distributed in Egypt and the Levant. The religious innovators Muhammad Abduh and Jamal al-Din al-Afghani were early writers of the newspaper. Upon the death of Bishara Takla, Dawud Barakat, a Lebanese journalist, was named editor of the daily in 1901.

82a512d3-aced-55a2-b8b4-370dfafb5ffc.name: *Théâtre de l'Opéra. "Aida". The banks of the Nile (act 3). Set by Jean-Louis Chéret*
82a512d3-aced-55a2-b8b4-370dfafb5ffc.artist: Engraver: Auguste Lepère; artists: Henry Scott, Jean-Louis Chéret
82a512d3-aced-55a2-b8b4-370dfafb5ffc.description2: Commissioned by Isma'il Pasha for the inauguration of the Suez Canal, Verdi's opera *Aida* was performed for the first time in Cairo in 1871, with great success. It recreated life at the time of the pharaohs, with the details and the plot developed by the archaeologist Mariette. *Aida* was performed in Paris from 1876, with a grand and successful performance at the Opéra Garnier in 1880.

83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.name: Lace skirt
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.author: Huda Kilani
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.description2: Skirt of light pink lace with black flowers, pursed from the middle, worn over a woman’s dress. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the various local costumes and rites, fashion and personal attire. This skirt was used by al-Druze women in Jordan. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.name: Traditional dress for a *shaykh* or *shaykha*
84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.materials: The original were made of silk, velvet, gemstones, cashmere, satin, gold, silver
84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.second_name: Costume of the shaykha and of the shaykh of Keserwan
84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.description2: Featured here is the traditional dress for the *shaykh* and *shaykha* of the Keserwan district. The *kubran* is an embroidered jacket (with or without sleeves) made of silk or velvet. The *gumbaz* is a long dress or coat embroidered with gold or silver and sometimes adorned with semi-precious jewels. It consisted of three panels and was split on either side of the body, beginning from the hip area. Other components of this traditional attire were a *mentiene* (blouse), the *shirwal* baggy trousers, a velvet or satin cape with gold or silver embroidery, and a long belt called a *shamle* or *zunnar* made of silk or cashmere depending on the season, and which was wrapped around the waist or hips.

854b0143-ae03-59b2-a467-18c4378eee8e.name: *Kahveci başı*

865fb995-6617-5b7a-9f9e-71a7a96732e5.keywords: Weaponry; sword; Arabian; Arab; weapon; arms; armours; costume; accessories; fashion; dance
865fb995-6617-5b7a-9f9e-71a7a96732e5.description2: Sword belonging to Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim. The sword’s sheath is made out of leather and gold. The sword handle is made from elephant ivory whilst the blade is a type of steel called ‘*al-jawhar*’ which is derived from the finest Arabian Damascus plate.

888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.name: Ring
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.author: Huda Kilani
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.keywords: Floral decoration; religious objects; waqf; Qur’an; Ottoman Baroque-Rococo
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.description2:
Thin silver ring with a squared black stone set in silver. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom.  
Jordan's economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for this purpose. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.name: Tabla
8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music
8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
8951f6af-b5d8-564b-983b-9fd818e52be8.description2: The *tabla*, also known as the *durbakke*, is a small hand drum very common in traditional Arabic music. It is shaped like a vase, and is covered at the top with goat skin. *Tabla*s are often beautifully decorated, with metal, bone inlay, or paint.

89881283-d829-5946-bd7c-505438d8c8c0.name: Costume for Cleopatra in the Ballets Russes production of *Cléopâtre*, 1918
89881283-d829-5946-bd7c-505438d8c8c0.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

89881283-d829-5946-bd7c-505438d8c8c0.artist: Sonia Terk Delaunay (born Russia, active France, 1885-1979)
89881283-d829-5946-bd7c-505438d8c8c0.keywords: Clothing; theatre; dance; fashion; abstract decoration; exoticism; textile; painting; coreography; abstract art; avant-garde
89881283-d829-5946-bd7c-505438d8c8c0.materials: Silk, sequins, mirror, beads, wool yarn, metallic thread braid, lamé
89881283-d829-5946-bd7c-505438d8c8c0.description2: The sets and many costumes for the 1909 *Cleopatre* were destroyed in a fire during the company’s 1917 South American tour, so painter Sonia Delaunay was commissioned to fashion new costumes for the principals. The artist’s palette of brilliant color, graphic design, and combination of textures resulted in costumes markedly different from the originals. Cleopatra’s luminous dress, reflecting the abstract forms in Sonia Delaunay’s paintings, as well as aspects of fashionable dress of the period, remains one of her most significant creations for the theatre.

89f4e566-e82c-56e3-b94a-d8bd68a1f680.name: *Tercüman*
89f4e566-e82c-56e3-b94a-d8bd68a1f680.keywords: costume; Orientalism; travel; traveller; fashion; court life

8a730c5e-8120-5c99-a9fa-3fffc09ae06e.name: *Théâtre Impérial du Châtelet. Aladdin and the magnificent lamp; the genies of the lamp (ballet).*
8a730c5e-8120-5c99-a9fa-3fffc09ae06e.artist: Engraver: Auguste Tricon; artist: Auguste Belin
8a730c5e-8120-5c99-a9fa-3fffc09ae06e.archival: ESTAMPES SCENES Aladin ou la lampe merveilleuse (1)
8a730c5e-8120-5c99-a9fa-3fffc09ae06e.description2: The tale of Aladdin became very popular following the rise of Orientalism in the 1820s, and became the subject of multiple adaptations for opera and for theatre. In 1863 Adolphe d'Ennery and Hector Crémieux also transformed it into a "féerie" (fairy play). This féerie, a genre which chose great legends as its subject and spanned many different mediums (ballet, on-stage special effects) was extremely popular in 1860s France.

8ad123be-79dd-59a7-84a8-ffc0f7c6d8e7.name: *James Robertson and His Brother-in-Law Felice Beato in Turkish Costume*
8ad123be-79dd-59a7-84a8-ffc0f7c6d8e7.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
8ad123be-79dd-59a7-84a8-ffc0f7c6d8e7.keywords: self-portrait; watercolour on photographs; Felice Beato
8ad123be-79dd-59a7-84a8-ffc0f7c6d8e7.description2: A self-portrait of James Robertson and his brother-in-law Felice Beato standing side by side and dressed in Turkish costume is an important work in the history of photography. This picture is in every sense a coloured counterpart of two other portrait photographs by Robertson first brought to light by Bahattin Öztuncay in 1991. The image of Felice Beato in this identical photograph is the only known picture of him in his youth.

8c28d282-9632-5ae4-81b1-ed79c1035940.name: Poem
8c28d282-9632-5ae4-81b1-ed79c1035940.keywords: Antonio Cappelletti; Emperor Franz Joseph; Cairo; Egypt
8c28d282-9632-5ae4-81b1-ed79c1035940.description2: This poem was written by Antonio Cappelletti in honour of Emperor Franz Joseph's visit to Cairo on 20 November 1869.

8ccd3080-01c6-56b9-82eb-95127eef1d1d.name: Robe
8ccd3080-01c6-56b9-82eb-95127eef1d1d.bibliography: Walter B. Denny, “Length of Fabric”, in Maryam D. Ekhtiar, Priscilla P. Soucek, Sheila R. Canby, and Navina Najat Haidar, eds., *Masterpieces from the Department of Islamic Art in The Metropolitan Museum of Art* (New York, 2011), pp. 320-1
8ccd3080-01c6-56b9-82eb-95127eef1d1d.keywords: Costume; dress; fashion; Ottoman influence; Turkish influence; design; tulip; floral decoration; vegetal decoration; Ottoman textiles
8ccd3080-01c6-56b9-82eb-95127eef1d1d.description2: The bold pattern of wavy vines, tulips and spear-shaped leaves on this robe designed by Mariano Fortuny, y Madrazo (1871-1949) is based on an imperial Ottoman silk of the 1560s. So appealing was the original Ottoman design that copies were produced in the 17th century and later, not only in textiles but also ceramic tiles. It is unclear whether Fortuny was familiar with the 16th century Ottoman lampas with metal-wrapped thread or with one of the textiles or tiles it inspired. Born in Spain, he was raised in Paris and Venice in a family that collected textiles and other artefacts. In his palazzo in Venice he not only designed fabrics and fashionable clothing but also invented new techniques of theatrical lighting and produced art in a variety of media. Since he lived in Venice with its long tradition of trade with the Ottoman Empire, he would have had extensive exposure to items from the Eastern Mediterranean. Also, from the late 1880s a range of textiles, carpets and other objects stored in the various Ottoman palaces in Istanbul were sold and found their way onto the European market.

8d0345df-1e22-5450-8f37-706dc5be7d91.name: A Woman from Cairo
8d0345df-1e22-5450-8f37-706dc5be7d91.holder: MIBACT | National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography “Luigi Pigorini”

8d0345df-1e22-5450-8f37-706dc5be7d91.description2: This photo from Enrico H. Giglioli's collection was taken by the Florentine naturalist during his travels around the world in 1865 and 1868 while advancing diplomatic and commercial relations between the newborn Italian state and the other nations. The images seem to have been created spontaneously to show ethnocentric diversity. The ethnographic photographs in the Giglioli's collection are part of the historical archive of the Pigorini Museum. The origins of scientific activity and conservation of Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the "Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography in Rome" within the buildings of the Roman College.

8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.name: Headdress
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.author: Huda Kilani
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.description2: Three bands of silver (800) chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head; 1/4 Ottoman coins (*barah*s) are fixed in the inner section of the band. This kind of jewellery was part of the dowry the groom gave to the bride. Dowries consisted mostly of silver jewellery because only the rich could afford gold jewellery. Thus, the financial status of the groom was highlighted by the jewellery he could give as a dowry and by the use of coins as pieces of jewellery for his wife.

8eb7973a-8c9e-5910-83bd-ad5e77872aba.name: *Algerians*
8eb7973a-8c9e-5910-83bd-ad5e77872aba.author: Dalila Orfali
8eb7973a-8c9e-5910-83bd-ad5e77872aba.description2: This study consists of a series of sketches depicting various Algerians. The subjects are mostly women, whose faces, wrapped in a traditional *haik*, are particularly interesting. According to experts only two paintings of this kind exist today. Before being acquired by the museum this study belonged to an important collection from the late 19th century. In 2003 it was published in the Australian scholar Roger Benjamin's collection dedicated to Auguste Renoir's Algerian period, *Renoir and Algeria*.

8f10719a-7586-5524-9036-a47811acc887.name: *Muhammad 'Ali Pasha*
8f10719a-7586-5524-9036-a47811acc887.keywords: Ruling Family; Rulers of Egypt; The Alawiyya Dynasty; Turks; The Ruling Elite
8f10719a-7586-5524-9036-a47811acc887.description2: Muhammad 'Ali Pasha, founder of Modern Egypt and Wali of Egypt in 1805. He was the head of the Alawiyya Dynasty that ruled Egypt from 1805 to 1952, and founder of modern Egypt. He came to Egypt in 1799 as part of a military unit to fight with the Turks – and the help of the British – to drive the French out of Egypt. However, the Turkish forces were defeated in 1799 in the Battle of Abu Qir.

8fde581f-45b3-50e0-854f-e74c4857e328.name: Hafiz Ibrahim
8fde581f-45b3-50e0-854f-e74c4857e328.dates: Born 1872 Dairut, Egypt; died 1932 Cairo, Egypt

92c6732e-264e-56fc-b2bd-43a71e310d3b.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
92c6732e-264e-56fc-b2bd-43a71e310d3b.materials: The original was made of silk and cashmere
92c6732e-264e-56fc-b2bd-43a71e310d3b.description2: This was the formal dress of the Emir of the Chouf district. It consists of traditional *shirwal* trousers and a silk jacket with embroidered patterns.

The arches, the dresses and the general decoration recall the illuminated pages of the 13th century illuminated books preserved in the Royal Collection and Library.

957ca713-c1c0-5491-8542-164f00239bf4.name: *Aladdin, or The Magnificent Lamp: sketch of the set for act 1 or act 2*
957ca713-c1c0-5491-8542-164f00239bf4.description2: The tale of Aladdin and his lamp was very popular in the theatre and the opera following the rise of Orientalism in the 1820s. Its first performance as an opera in 1822 was so successful that gas was used for the first time ever at the Opéra de Paris, to light up the lamp on stage.

96e36ed2-2da9-5b5a-b4bb-79b6897cf288.name: Portrait of Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq
96e36ed2-2da9-5b5a-b4bb-79b6897cf288.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
96e36ed2-2da9-5b5a-b4bb-79b6897cf288.description2: Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq was born in 1804 in the 'Ashqut (Keserwan) district, and received his primary education in Hadath (Ba'abda), and his secondary education in 'Ayn Warka School. Here, he studied both foreign languages and Arabic literature. He was later converted to Protestantism by American missionaries in the region. He moved to Egypt in 1825, and then to Malta in 1834, where he lived for 14 years. During this period he became the head of the American Printing Press, and started publishing his own books. From Malta, he travelled to London, Paris and Tunis, where he converted to Islam and changed his name to Shaykh Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq. In 1857, he began publishing his newspaper whilst he continued to edit his books. He died on 20 September 1889, and was buried in Lebanon, in Hazmiyya.

9729e384-0aab-59c6-bb73-2a5621d81218.name: Bridal headdress (*Tepelak* – tas)
9729e384-0aab-59c6-bb73-2a5621d81218.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist
9729e384-0aab-59c6-bb73-2a5621d81218.keywords: Head-dress; tepelak; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; tughra; marriage; wedding; fashion; costume
9729e384-0aab-59c6-bb73-2a5621d81218.materials: Gilt silver, casting, filigree, adornment with small coins
9729e384-0aab-59c6-bb73-2a5621d81218.description2: Jewellery worn on the head included diverse types of metal articles which served to support the hat or scarf and also had an apotropaic function in addition to their decorative one. Especially noteworthy head-pieces were *tepelaks*. These are headdresses of round form, sometimes slightly concave, abundantly adorned with chains, smaller or larger silver coins and with *trepkas* (tiny ornaments in diverse forms – round, leaf-shaped, rectangular, heart-shaped, etc.). *Tepelaks* used to be worn everywhere in Macedonia, particularly in the Kumanovo, Skopje, Gostivar and Gevgelija regions, as well as within Vlachs. This piece of bridal *tepelak-tas* was made by application of filigree technique. It is abundantly decorated with coins suspended on tiny chains.

97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.name: Wedding dress
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.author: Huda Kilani
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.materials: Linen with silk; hand weaving, hand embroidered, natural dyes
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.description2: The main fabric of this wedding dress is linen with silk selvedge stripes, with red and yellow taffeta inserts in the sleeves and skirt; the chest panel is couched with gilt cord and yellow, green and purple silk cord, and filled with multi-coloured stain and herringbone stitches. Palestinian weavers used manual spindles to prepare the cotton and linen threads imported from Egypt. Ashkelon weavers used light vertical hand looms (*Majdalawi* looms) to produce linen fabrics, while silk fabrics were spindled, died and woven in Syria. The Jordanian economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on trade and crafts; new waves of people started to come to Jordan to participate in those industries. This object shows the diverse population composition of Jordan at that time, through personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

997dbce0-9881-50bc-95f4-a36fa4a0fb35.name: Portrait of Shaykh Nasif al-Yaziji
997dbce0-9881-50bc-95f4-a36fa4a0fb35.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
997dbce0-9881-50bc-95f4-a36fa4a0fb35.keywords: Writer; Scientist; College, Renaissance; Arabic; Lebanese
997dbce0-9881-50bc-95f4-a36fa4a0fb35.description2: Shaykh Nasif al-Yaziji was born in March 1800 in Kfarshima (Ba'abda). He wrote his first poems age ten, and after mastering the sciences became the assistant to Emir Bashir Shihab II for 12 years. In 1840 he moved to Beirut and dedicated himself to writing. He also became a professor at al-Bustani's National School and later at the Syrian Protestant College (now the American University of Beirut). He stayed here until 1869, when he fell ill and retired. He died in February 1871, forty days after the death of his oldest son. He is most famous for his work *Majma' al-Bahrayn*.

9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.name: Bridal breast jewellery (*Chaprag*)
9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist
9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.keywords: Breast ornament; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; accessories; costume; wedding; marriage
9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.third_name: Chaprag – Nevestinski ukras za na gadi
9a135c4c-830c-5fdd-a5e6-61129754ecfd.description2: This exquisite article called a *chaprag* shows the exceptional skill and inventiveness of the unknown goldsmith, who makes each piece of jewellery a virtual work of art in itself. The *chaprag* is a breast ornament consisting of a round plate and tiny chains. It is executed in filigree technique and adorned with decorative stones. Besides its decorative function, it was applied for the purpose of fastening the cleavage of the tunic. It was characteristic of the Ohrid-Prespa region, that is, the areas of Ohridsko Pole, Strushko Pole and Debarski Drimkol.

9a2b6628-fecf-51cc-8501-edcd12db0810.name: Portrait of Wadih Sabra
9a2b6628-fecf-51cc-8501-edcd12db0810.holder: Lebanese National Higher Conservatory of Music
9a2b6628-fecf-51cc-8501-edcd12db0810.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
9a2b6628-fecf-51cc-8501-edcd12db0810.description2: Wadih Sabra was the composer of the Ottoman anthem, used today as the Lebanese National anthem. He also established the Institute of Music in Beirut, as decreed by Sultan 'Abd al-Hamid in 1910, and founded the National Conservatory. He was the founder of the first musical-scientific journal of its kind in the Arab region, and wrote the first Arabic language opera.

9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.name: Belt
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.author: Huda Kilani
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.description2: A Circassian belt with 15 silver and niello-decorated buckles connected together to form the belt; there is a rosette shape at the end with locking mechanism and three dangling silver tassels. This belt, together with the dagger, was an accessory forming the traditional male Circassian dress. The Circassians used to carry daggers which were an essential part of the national dress. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries with which they had spiritual and religious links.

9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.name: Brass head of flagpole
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.author: Huda Kilani
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.description2: A cultic item with Arabic calligraphy mentioning God and his prophet Muhammad made of casted brass; fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized that would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

a12c9928-1d6f-5b1e-814c-74692d5b8de6.name: Arabi, Sayed Ahmed Pasha (1841–1911)
a12c9928-1d6f-5b1e-814c-74692d5b8de6.description2: Portrait of minister Sayed Ahmed Pasha Arabi (Urabi). In 1882, the war minister took power in Egypt and demanded an end to the financial control imposed by the UK and France. This led to an intervention by the British Navy under Admiral Seymour, who defeated the Egyptian army.

a2ba32a3-7747-5b54-b011-e71d3a84e08c.name: Dress
a2ba32a3-7747-5b54-b011-e71d3a84e08c.description: Pink silk twill dress lined with cotton, long-sleeved and high-waisted. The neckline is round in the front and triangle-shaped in the back. The upper bodice area is boned. Both breasts are marked with a U-shaped pleating. The skirt is soberly straight in front but it gains volume towards the back, ending in a short trail. The dress is fastened with invisible hooks at the back and adorned with buttons covered in the same silk fabric. The lower end presents a wide multi-coloured paisley frieze; each drop is composed of minute woven flowers. This elegant dress is a late variation of Empire dresses; the slender high-waisted silhouette is the same, but the fabric is thicker, the neckline has turned more modest and the long sleeves go down to cover part of the hands.

a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.name: Part of a veil
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.author: Huda Kilani
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.keywords: Gold; Ottoman coins; above the nose; piece of cloth
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.description2: Five lines of gold ¼ Ottoman lira and other type of coins sewn together on a piece of cloth; such pieces were usually affixed above the nose on the veils, *burqu'*, of women of Beer Sheba. Fashion, local costumes and rites in the territories of Jordan and Palestine show identical elements, as this veil illustrates. It is one of the many examples of jewellery made with Ottoman coins to decorate veils and dresses. Jewellery was an important accessory for married women because pieces of jewellery constituted part of the dowry their husbands gave them for marriage. Jewellery was also a symbol of financial prestige: the more precious it was, the richer the husband’s family. Silver jewellery was the most common because only rich people could afford gold jewellery.
